(a) typically developing children can reliably be classified into distinct subgroups based on their neuropsychological performance and (b) some of the heterogenous neuropsychological subpopulations of children with ADHD are similar to the subgroups of typically developing youth, suggesting that ADHD is not an entirely distinct neuropsychological disorder.

(a) typically developing youth and children with ADHD are not a homogenous population, but can be divided into several subgroups based on neuropsychological profiles, and (b) the heterogeneity in the children with ADHD is not random, but is "nested" in the variation that exists in the typically developing youth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the existing classification of developmental psychiatric disorders can be improved.
the identification of subgroups within a typically developing sample and the potential for these subgroups to inform heterogeneity in individuals who have been diagnosed with ADHD.
identifying the heterogeneity that may underlie the current diagnostic classifications and to determine whether this heterogeneity can inform the development of more accurate diagnostic algorithms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the DSM classification scheme is not a sufficient description of the neuropsychological heterogeneities in either typically developing or clinical populations.

the neuropsychology of children with ADHD is not a homogeneous disorder, but rather is composed of several subgroups that are distinct from typically developing children, as well as distinct from each other.
there are distinct subtypes of neuropsychological function that can be identified in both typically developing and ADHD youth, and these subtypes can inform the clinical presentation of ADHD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the heterogeneity that exists in the typically developing population is not random and can be used as a framework for understanding the heterogeneity that is present in children with developmental disorders such as ADHD.
the neuropsychological heterogeneities in typically developing youth are not simply a "background noise" but are the foundation for understanding the heterogeneity in children diagnosed with ADHD.
the heterogeneity that is present in typically developing children can help us understand the heterogeneity in children who are diagnosed with ADHD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need to re-examine our assumptions about the nature of the diagnostic categories we use in clinical and translational research.

the current DSM categories may be too coarse to capture the heterogeneity of ADHD and other disorders, and that more refined subgroups may be necessary to advance our understanding and treatment of these disorders.
